add: The frequentist approach to quantile trend filtering was developed by \citet{brantley2020baseline}, who combined the check loss of \citet{koenker1978regression} with the discrete difference penalty of \citet{tibshirani2014adaptive} and solved the resulting nonsmooth convex program via the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Their estimator scales well to large signals and inherits the locally adaptive properties of $\ell_1$ trend filtering. Theoretical properties, including risk bounds, have been studied by \citet{madrid2022risk}. This approach provides a natural benchmark for estimation, but its output is a point estimate at a selected penalty level. Regularization selection, for example through an extended Bayesian information criterion, and uncertainty quantification require procedures beyond the ADMM optimization itself.

We develop an adaptive, fully Bayesian extension of quantile trend filtering computed by ADMM. The connection is exact: under an asymmetric Laplace likelihood and a global Laplace prior on the trend differences, the conditional posterior mode at $\sigma=1$ and fixed $\lambda$ coincides with the frequentist estimator. We extend this formulation by learning the regularization strength and likelihood scale jointly with the trend, and use ADMM within posterior sampling to retain its useful computational structure. This retains a posterior distribution over the trend while avoiding the growing collection of latent-scale updates and repeated matrix computations that make conventional augmented Gibbs implementations costly for long time series. Section~\ref{subsec:individual} establishes the mode equivalence.

Related progress on Bayesian quantile regression in additive and spline settings has been made by \citet{fasiolo2021fast}, though their approach targets smooth additive models rather than piecewise polynomial trends of arbitrary order. The analogous trajectory for mean trend filtering has been traced by Heng, Zhou, and Chi, who placed the $\ell_1$ trend filtering problem of \citet{tibshirani2014adaptive} in a Bayesian framework using proximal Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques \citep{pereyra2016proximal}. The quantile setting introduces an additional computational difficulty: both the check loss and the difference penalty are nonsmooth. The challenge is therefore to preserve the useful optimization structure while making joint posterior inference computationally practical.

The Bayesian quantile trend filtering method of \citet{onizuka2024fast} illustrates this computational challenge. Its Gibbs sampler uses latent-variable representations of the likelihood and shrinkage prior, requiring observation-level latent updates, local-scale updates for the trend differences, and a Gaussian trend update with a precision matrix that changes each iteration. These updates support flexible local shrinkage, especially under the horseshoe prior, but impose substantial computational overhead. In the supplied implementation, dense inversion and Gaussian simulation remain a bottleneck even with the tested sparse option enabled. Our formulation instead uses one global regularization parameter per quantile and an ADMM proximal system that permits factorization reuse.

The same authors also propose a faster mean-field variational Bayes (VB) approximation, together with a calibration procedure for its uncertainty summaries \citep{onizuka2024fast}. In exploratory runs beyond the $n=100$ reference setting, we encountered numerical failures in the public VB implementation. This implementation-specific observation provides additional motivation for a sampling alternative; our comparisons focus on estimation accuracy and computational performance rather than a quantitative assessment of uncertainty calibration.

The present paper combines the mode connection with a computational use of ADMM: the same class of $\ell_1$ trend filtering subproblems becomes the engine of posterior simulation. We construct a three-block Gibbs scheme that updates the single global regularization parameter $\lambda$ and the likelihood scale $\sigma$ from conjugate full conditionals, and updates the trend through a proximal Metropolis-adjusted Langevin (P-MALA) step \citep{pereyra2016proximal}. This formulation retains the local adaptation induced by the $\ell_1$ difference penalty without introducing a separate random shrinkage scale for every difference or a latent variable for every observation. For each quantile, only two scalar hyperparameters are sampled in addition to the trend. The proximal subproblems are solved using ADMM. In the constrained formulation, their coefficient matrix depends only on the difference operator and fixed algorithmic parameters, permitting reuse of a banded factorization. With sparse operations and a bounded number of inner ADMM iterations, the work per outer iteration is linear in the sample size. The advantage is thus a simpler hierarchy and reusable optimization structure, together with posterior inference for the trend and its regularization strength.

\item We develop an adaptive Bayesian extension of the frequentist quantile trend filtering estimator: its conditional posterior mode recovers the ADMM solution at $\sigma=1$ and fixed $\lambda$, while the full hierarchy learns both parameters jointly with the trend and propagates their uncertainty into posterior summaries.

\item We use ADMM within proximal posterior sampling, with one global regularization parameter per quantile and no observation-level likelihood augmentation. The constrained proximal system permits reuse of a banded factorization; sparse operations give linear work in $n$ for a fixed inner iteration budget, avoiding the dense inverse and Gaussian simulation used by the supplied Gibbs benchmark.

\item Through a comprehensive simulation study spanning four signal structures, three noise distributions, three difference orders, and both interior and extreme quantile levels, we demonstrate that the proposed sampler delivers accuracy comparable to or better than the competitive Bayesian approach of \citet{onizuka2024fast}, with posterior uncertainty summaries and reduced computational overhead relative to the supplied dense Gibbs implementation, and that it does so using a single global penalty parameter rather than the per-coordinate local shrinkage employed by competing priors, which simplifies the prior specification and the resulting sampler.

\paragraph{Connection to frequentist quantile trend filtering.}
For $\sigma=1$ and fixed $\lambda>0$, the conditional posterior mode satisfies
\begin{equation}
\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MAP}}(\lambda)
\in \arg\min_{\theta\in\R^n}
\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\rho_\tau(y_i-\theta_i)
+\lambda\norm{D\theta}_1\right\}.
\label{eq:map_qtf}
\end{equation}

The optimization problem on the right is the frequentist quantile trend filtering problem of \citet{brantley2020baseline}, solved by ADMM. The equivalence concerns the conditional mode at fixed hyperparameters; posterior means and summaries obtained by integrating over $\lambda$ and $\sigma$ need not coincide with that estimate. Our Bayesian extension assigns priors to both parameters and infers them jointly with $\theta$, making regularization and likelihood scale data-adaptive while retaining the same check-loss and difference-penalty structure.

Quantile trend filtering estimates time-varying conditional quantiles through a check loss and an $\ell_1$ difference penalty, with efficient frequentist estimation available via ADMM \citep{brantley2020baseline}. We develop an adaptive, fully Bayesian extension of this estimator. Under an asymmetric Laplace likelihood and a global Laplace difference prior, the conditional posterior mode at unit likelihood scale and fixed regularization parameter coincides with the frequentist ADMM solution. Assigning priors to both parameters allows the regularization strength and likelihood scale to be inferred jointly with the trend. A three-block Gibbs scheme combines their conjugate updates with a proximal Metropolis-adjusted Langevin (P-MALA) trend update \citep{pereyra2016proximal}, using ADMM to solve the required trend filtering subproblems. The hierarchy uses one global regularization parameter per quantile, without observation-level likelihood augmentation or separate random scales for the trend differences. In the constrained proximal formulation, a fixed banded system permits factorization reuse and linear work in the sample size for a fixed number of inner ADMM iterations.

Simulation studies spanning piecewise constant, varying smoothness, and smooth signals under Gaussian, Beta, and mixed normal noise examine estimation accuracy at interior and extreme quantile levels, with posterior uncertainty summaries obtained from the sampled trends. The results show competitive estimation relative to the Bayesian approach of \citet{onizuka2024fast}. The simpler hierarchy and ADMM computation provide a practical route to extending the frequentist benchmark to joint Bayesian inference.

A central motivation for the proposed approach is to make Bayesian inference practical while retaining the optimization structure of frequentist quantile trend filtering. The supplied Gibbs implementation of \citet{onizuka2024fast} forms a dense inverse and uses dense Gaussian simulation at each iteration. Our audit found that its sparse option still enters this dense computational path in the benchmark environment, so enabling that option does not remove the principal bottleneck. The augmented hierarchy also updates observation-level latent variables and local prior scales, whereas our formulation samples one global regularization parameter and one likelihood scale per quantile in addition to the trend.

This distinction should be separated from an asymptotic claim about all Gibbs implementations. At fixed difference order, a Gaussian draw based directly on the banded precision can be computed in $O(n)$ work without forming an inverse, although the changing weights generally require a new numerical factorization each iteration. For our constrained proximal system, $\mathbf{A}=\gamma^{-1}\mathbf{I}+\rho D^\top D+\rho\mathbf{I}$ is independent of the sampled parameters, allowing factor reuse when $D$, $\gamma$, and $\rho$ remain fixed. Sparse operations give $O(nJ)$ work for $J$ inner ADMM sweeps, plus linear setup and sufficient-statistic calculations. Practical comparisons must account for the inner iteration count, factorization reuse in the actual implementation, and mixing of the complete chain. Timing per outer iteration alone does not establish cost per effective posterior draw.

Treating the ALD scale $\sigma$ as an unknown parameter rather than fixing it at the optimization convention of unity is a substantive modeling decision with several consequences. Within the Gibbs scheme, $\sigma$ and $\lambda$ interact with the trend estimate in complementary ways: $\sigma$ calibrates the effective likelihood temperature, controlling how sharply the gradient of the smoothed check loss responds to residuals, while $\lambda$ calibrates the effective smoothness penalty. Decoupling these two sources of regularization allows each to adapt to a different aspect of the data --- noise level and signal roughness respectively --- and prevents the single tuning parameter of the frequentist formulation from having to absorb both roles simultaneously. Learning $\sigma$ allows the likelihood scale to respond to the data, but does not by itself guarantee frequentist coverage when the asymmetric Laplace likelihood is misspecified. Posterior sampling avoids the additional mean-field approximation used by VB; coverage remains a separate question, as recognized by the calibration approach of \citet{onizuka2024fast}. A practical caveat is that $\sigma$ and $\lambda$ are not fully separable in their effects on the posterior for $\theta$: both appear in the effective curvature seen by the P-MALA proposal, and under severe misspecification their joint posterior may exhibit a soft ridge. The weakly informative prior $\sigma \sim \mathrm{IG}(0.1, 0.1)$ is sufficient to regularize this in all settings considered, but sensitivity of the posterior to this prior choice warrants attention in applications where the noise distribution is far from symmetric or unimodal.
